why.correct: The Change row is x times each coefficient, negative for species used up. H₂ has coefficient 3: −3x.
options: Right: three H₂ react for every N₂, so H₂ falls three times as fast.
This ignores the coefficient 3 on H₂.
H₂ is a reactant in a net forward reaction, so it is used up: the sign is negative.
The coefficient multiplies x; it does not divide it.

why.correct: Species react and form in the mole ratio of the balanced equation, so every change is x times a coefficient.
options: Right: once you know how much N₂ reacted, stoichiometry gives the change in H₂ and NH₃.
They change in the ratio 1 : 3 : 2, not by equal amounts; that is why the coefficients multiply x.
x is the change for a species with coefficient 1. The equilibrium values are Initial + Change.
That makes unit conversion easy but does not explain why a single unknown works.

why.correct: Check the approximation: x / [initial] × 100% = 0.089 / 0.200 × 100% ≈ 45%. Over about 5%, x cannot be dropped and the equation must be solved exactly.
options: Right: the approximation is only safe when x is a few percent of the starting concentration or less.
Being smaller than 0.200 is not enough; x must be negligible next to it (under about 5%).
K < 1 alone does not guarantee x is small. Here K is only moderately small compared with the concentration.
Starting with no products is the usual case for the approximation. It fails here because K is not small enough.

why.correct: Substituting your answers into the K expression is a quick check: an equilibrium mixture gives Q = K.
options: Right: (0.0717)² / 0.128 ≈ 0.040. Q equals K, so the mixture is at equilibrium.
Substituting into K gives K back, not x. And the approximation was not valid.
The starting concentration is not what the K expression returns.
If the solution is right, Q equals K. A smaller Q would mean an arithmetic error.

why.correct: The approximation replaces (initial − x) by (initial) when x is tiny. It never replaces x itself by zero.
options: Right: 0.10 − 2x ≈ 0.10 is fine, but x terms standing alone must stay, or nothing is left to solve for.
Setting x to zero on top makes Q = 0, which can never equal K. Only x inside a sum or difference may be dropped.
Dropping x from "0.10 − 2x" changes the value by a few percent; dropping it from "(2x)²x" changes it to zero. They are not the same.
The number of species does not matter. What matters is whether x is small next to the number it is subtracted from.

why.correct: The 5% rule: the amount subtracted (here 2x) should be under about 5% of the starting concentration. If it is, the approximation was justified.
options: Right: 2x = 2.7 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M, which is 2.7% of 0.10 M.
A positive x is needed, but it does not show the approximation is valid.
A small K makes the approximation likely to work, but you still verify it with the answer.
x and K are different kinds of quantity; the test compares x with the starting concentration.

why.correct: When K is much smaller than the starting concentration terms, little reactant is used, so x is small relative to the initial amount.
options: Right: a tiny K means a reactant-favored equilibrium, so the change from the starting amount is small.
Starting with no products tells you the direction (forward), not how far the reaction goes.
Coefficients appear in the change row but do not decide whether x is small.
The size of the concentration alone does not decide it; the ratio of K to the concentration does.

why.correct: Compare Q with K before writing the Change row. Q > K means net reverse: the reactant side gains +x and the product side loses −x.
options: Right: Q = (0.200)² / (0.0500)² = 16.0 > K, so the net reaction goes in reverse: reactants form, products are used.
This assumes a forward reaction. Check Q first: Q = 16.0 is greater than K, so the reaction runs in reverse.
Every species cannot decrease; atoms must go somewhere. One side forms while the other is used.
Having all species present does not mean equilibrium. Q = 16.0 ≠ K = 1.56.

why.correct: Direction first, then the ICE table, then solve and check. The check catches a bad approximation or a sign error.
x is small when K is much smaller than the starting concentration terms. Always confirm with the 5% check afterward.
options: Right: K is tiny compared with the starting concentration, so x will be a very small fraction of 0.50 M.
K is large compared with the concentration here, so a large fraction reacts.
K > 1 means products are favored; most of the reactant reacts.
K near 1 leaves appreciable amounts of both sides; x is not small.

why.correct: x / [A]₀ × 100% = (6.3 × 10⁻³ / 0.100) × 100% = 6.3%. That is just over 5%, so the approximation is borderline; solving exactly is safer.
If x is more than about 5% of the starting concentration, the approximation is not reliable. Solve with the quadratic formula (or by successive approximation).
options: Right: above about 5%, dropping x from 0.100 − x makes a noticeable error.
The usual threshold is about 5%, set so the error stays within the precision of the data.
K is fixed by the reaction and temperature; you cannot change it to suit the math.
There is no such correction. Solve the full equation instead.

why.correct: With K fixed, x ≈ √(K[A]₀). More starting reactant gives more product but a smaller percent reacted.

variables.name: [B] at equilibrium
variables.why: With x small, x² ≈ K[A]₀, so doubling [A]₀ raises x (by a factor of √2).

why.correct: Equilibrium is reached when the particle counts stop changing. The first two identical snapshots are at 40 s and 60 s.
options: Right: the counts at 40 s and 60 s are both 4 W and 4 W₂, so the composition has stopped changing.
The counts change between 20 s (6 W, 3 W₂) and 40 s (4 W, 4 W₂), so the system was still reacting at 20 s.
The system is at equilibrium at 60 s, but its composition was already the same at 40 s.
At 0 s there is no W₂, so the forward reaction is about to change the composition.

why.correct: 4 particles × 0.10 mol = 0.40 mol W; [W] = 0.40 mol / 2.0 L = 0.20 M.
A product count that is rising means the forward reaction is faster than the reverse.
options: Right: W₂ is building up (0 to 3), so dimers form faster than they split.
Equal rates would leave the counts unchanged, but W falls from 12 to 6.
That would make W₂ split faster than it forms, but W₂ is increasing.
At 0 s the forward rate is at its largest: there are 12 W particles and no W₂.

why.correct: K<sub>c</sub> uses molarities. Here the top has one concentration term and the bottom two, so V and the moles per particle do not cancel; skipping the conversion gives the wrong value.
options: Right: K = (n/V) / (n/V)² = V/n here, so the volume, 2.0 L, and the 0.10 mol per particle stay in the answer.
Counts can be used once they are turned into concentrations; and when the gas moles are equal on both sides, they even give K directly.
Each W₂ is one molecule, so it counts once as W₂. The issue is units, not how W₂ is counted.
K<sub>c</sub> is defined with molar concentrations; only that version is the equilibrium constant.

why.correct: Here the gas moles are equal on both sides (2 and 2), so the volume cancels and counts can go straight into Q. A box is at equilibrium when Q = K = 4.0.
options: Q = 2² / (3 × 3) = 0.44 < K, so it will react forward.
Q = 6² / (1 × 1) = 36 > K, so it will react in reverse.
Right: Q = 4² / (4 × 1) = 4.0 = K. Unequal amounts of X₂ and Y₂ do not matter; only Q = K does.

why.correct: Compare Q with K. Box 3 has Q = 36 > K, so the net reaction goes in reverse until Q falls to 4.0.
options: Right: Q = 36 > 4.0, so the net reaction runs in reverse and XY breaks down.
Q > K means too much product; the net reaction must lower Q by using up XY.
Abundance alone does not decide; Q = 36 is not K = 4.0.
The net reverse reaction makes X₂ and Y₂; they increase.

why.correct: Two conditions: atoms are conserved (each X₂ + Y₂ that reacts makes 2 XY), and the final Q equals K.
options: Right: one X₂ and one Y₂ react to give 2 XY (atoms conserved), and Q = 16/4 = 4.0 = K.
This adds 2 XY without using any X₂ or Y₂, so atoms are not conserved.
This runs the reaction in reverse, but Box 2 has Q < K, so it must go forward.
Atoms are conserved, but Q = 36 overshoots K = 4.0.

why.correct: When the total coefficients of gases are equal on both sides, every V cancels from Q or K, so particle counts work directly.
options: Right: Q = (n<sub>XY</sub>/V)² / ((n<sub>X₂</sub>/V)(n<sub>Y₂</sub>/V)) = n<sub>XY</sub>² / (n<sub>X₂</sub>n<sub>Y₂</sub>).
Counts become concentrations only after dividing by volume; the volume cancels only in special cases like this one.
Equal volumes let you compare boxes, but for a single box it is the equal gas moles that make V cancel.
The value of K has nothing to do with whether counts can be used.

why.correct: At equilibrium (60 s on), [A] = 0.40 M and [B] = 0.80 M. K<sub>c</sub> = [B]² / [A] = (0.80)² / 0.40 = 1.6.
Compare changes, not final values: ΔB = +0.80 M, ΔA = −0.40 M, ratio 2 : 1.
options: Right: the changes are in the ratio 2 : 1, the coefficients.
True here, but final values depend on K and the starting amounts; the ratio of the changes is what shows the coefficients.
They always level off together at equilibrium; that does not show the 2 : 1 ratio.
That only shows B is a product present at the start in no amount.

why.correct: On a concentration-time graph, equilibrium is where every curve is horizontal. Where curves cross has no special meaning.
options: Right: the crossing only marks equal concentrations at one instant; both curves are still changing there.
Equal concentrations are not equal rates, and the curves are still steep at the crossing.
The reaction continues changing until about 60 s.
The curves need not meet. Equilibrium shows up as flat lines, which they become.

why.correct: Q<sub>c</sub> = [B]² / [A] = (0.36)² / 0.62 = 0.21, less than K = 1.6, consistent with the net forward reaction still under way.
Equilibrium is constant composition: the counts of each species do not change from snapshot to snapshot.
options: Right: at equilibrium the composition is constant, though individual particles keep reacting.
An equilibrium mixture contains reactants and products.
Equilibrium means constant counts, not equal counts.
Particles keep moving and reacting; only the counts stay the same.

why.correct: Only an equilibrium mixture gives K. Counts become concentrations through moles and volume; then use the expression.
A sudden vertical jump in one curve means that substance was added (or removed, for a drop). Gradual changes afterward are the system’s response.
options: Right: [Cl₂] jumps straight up at 50 s while the other two do not jump.
Added PCl₅ would make the PCl₅ curve jump. It rises gradually, as a result of the shift.
A temperature change does not make one concentration jump; the curves would bend smoothly to new values.
Halving the volume would make all three concentrations jump at once.

why.correct: Adding a product makes the system shift toward reactants, partly using up what was added. It does not undo the change completely.
options: Right: [Cl₂] and [PCl₃] fall while [PCl₅] rises, the reverse direction, which partly uses up the added Cl₂.
More Cl₂ forming would push [Cl₂] even higher. It falls after the jump.
K is unchanged, but Q has changed, so the system must react until Q = K again.
The shift only partly counteracts the change: [Cl₂] ends above its old value.

why.correct: Before the change: [PCl₃] = 0.072 M, [PCl₅] = 0.128 M. PCl₃ fell by 0.033 M, and the coefficients are 1 : 1, so PCl₅ rose by the same: 0.128 + 0.033 = 0.161 M.
K depends only on temperature. A concentration change shifts the equilibrium position, not the constant.
options: Right: the temperature did not change, so K did not change. The concentrations rearranged to fit the same K.
Adding Cl₂ changed Q, not K. The system shifted until Q equaled the original K.
A shift changes concentrations, not K.
The added Cl₂ is never all used up, and K is defined at any equilibrium.

why.correct: Adding a product shifts the equilibrium toward reactants. The added species ends higher than before, the other product lower, the reactant higher; K is unchanged.

variables.name: [PCl<sub>5</sub>]
variables.why: The reverse shift made more PCl₅.

variables.name: [PCl<sub>3</sub>]
variables.why: The reverse shift used some PCl₃.

variables.name: K<sub>c</sub>
variables.why: Same temperature, same K.

why.correct: For an endothermic reaction, heat acts like a reactant: adding heat shifts the equilibrium forward (blue), removing heat shifts it back (pink).
options: Right: heating shifts the equilibrium toward the blue product, so the forward reaction absorbs heat.
If it were exothermic, heating would shift toward the reactants and turn the tube pink. It turned blue.
The colors show where equilibrium lies, not how fast it is reached.
The color changed with temperature, so the equilibrium position did.

why.correct: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s) removes a reactant. The equilibrium shifts toward the side that makes Cl⁻: the pink side.
options: Right: lowering [Cl⁻], a reactant, makes the system shift in reverse to replace some of it.
The white solid is AgCl. The color change comes from the shift, not from silver joining a cobalt ion.
A few drops of solution barely dilute it. The precipitate shows Cl⁻ is being removed.
Nitrate is a spectator ion here; Ag⁺ is the active ion.

why.correct: Temperature is the one change that alters K. For an endothermic forward reaction, a higher temperature means a larger K.
options: Right: raising the temperature of an endothermic reaction increases K, which is why the mixture shifts toward the blue product.
K stays the same for concentration changes, but a temperature change alters K itself.
A shift toward products at higher temperature means K got larger, not smaller.
K is constant only at a fixed temperature.

why.correct: Adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium toward the products, partly using up what was added.
options: Right: the system uses some of the added Cl⁻, making more blue CoCl₄²⁻.
A few drops at room temperature have little heating effect; tube 4 is not in a bath.
Adding a reactant changes Q, not K.
The drops add a little water, if anything. The key change is the added Cl⁻.

why.correct: Le Châtelier’s principle: a change in concentration, volume or temperature makes the equilibrium shift to partly counteract it. A catalyst causes no shift.

variables.name: The volume of the container is halved
variables.why: Smaller volume favors the side with fewer gas molecules: 2 NH₃ versus 4 reactant molecules.

variables.name: The temperature is raised
variables.why: The forward reaction is exothermic, so heat acts as a product; adding heat shifts the equilibrium in reverse.

variables.name: A catalyst is added
variables.why: A catalyst speeds both directions equally; the equilibrium amounts do not change.

variables.name: Some H<sub>2</sub> is removed
variables.why: Removing a reactant shifts the equilibrium in reverse to replace some of it.

why.correct: Volume changes shift an equilibrium only when the gas moles differ on the two sides. Inert gases at constant volume and catalysts cause no shift.

variables.why: Both sides have 2 mol of gas, so a volume change affects reactants and products equally and causes no shift.

variables.name: Argon is added at constant volume
variables.why: An inert gas at constant volume changes no partial pressure or concentration of the reacting gases.

variables.name: More I<sub>2</sub> is added
variables.why: Adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium forward.

why.correct: Only temperature changes K. For an exothermic reaction (heat is a product), lowering the temperature increases K.
options: Right: for an exothermic reaction, cooling favors the products and increases K.
This shifts the equilibrium forward but does not change K.
This shifts toward fewer gas moles (products), but K stays the same.
A catalyst changes neither K nor the equilibrium position.

why.correct: Compression doubles every concentration first. Then the equilibrium shifts toward the side with fewer gas molecules, partly counteracting the change. [NO₂] ends higher than before the change but lower than right after it.
options: Right: halving the volume doubles [NO₂] instantly; the shift toward fewer gas molecules then lowers it partway.
The first effect is compression, which doubles [NO₂]. The shift comes after and only partly undoes it.
The system responds: it shifts toward N₂O₄ (fewer gas molecules), lowering [NO₂] somewhat.
K is unchanged, but the concentrations are not.

why.correct: Count only gas moles for volume changes (the solid does not count), and treat heat as a reactant for an endothermic reaction.
options: Right: the forward reaction is endothermic, so heat acts as a reactant.
Right: products have 2 mol gas, reactants 1 mol gas, so more room favors the products.
A pure solid does not appear in Q, so adding it causes no shift.
A catalyst causes no shift.

why.correct: K depends only on temperature. Adding a reactant disturbs the equilibrium (topic 7.10 shows how to state this with Q), and the system shifts forward.
options: Right: the shift happens because the mixture is out of balance with the same K, not because K changed.
Concentration changes never change K. Only temperature does.
K is unchanged, and adding a reactant shifts toward products.
N₂ is a reactant here; adding it does shift the equilibrium.

why.correct: After a concentration change, compare the new Q with the unchanged K. Q > K: net reverse.
options: Right: adding NO₂ raised Q to 2.3 × 10⁻² while K stayed 4.6 × 10⁻³.
K does not change with concentration. The added NO₂ changes Q.
A faster reverse reaction makes N₂O₄, not NO₂. And a justification should compare Q with K.
Q = 2.3 × 10⁻² is larger than K = 4.6 × 10⁻³, not smaller.

why.correct: Volume changes alter every concentration, and Q changes whenever the gas coefficients differ. Q < K means net forward, toward more gas molecules, consistent with Le Châtelier.
options: Right: Q = [NO₂]²/[N₂O₄] has two factors on top and one on the bottom; halving all of them halves Q, to 2.3 × 10<sup>−3</sup>.
Equal halving cancels only when the exponents on top and bottom match. Here they are 2 and 1.
A larger volume favors more gas moles. The products side has 2 mol gas versus 1.
Volume does not change K; it changes Q.

why.correct: Q = (0.0136)² / 0.0200 = 9.2 × 10<sup>−3</sup> > K, so the net reaction goes in reverse: NO₂ is used to form N₂O₄.
options: Right: removing N₂O₄ lowered the denominator, so Q rose above K; the reverse reaction uses NO₂ to re-form N₂O₄.
Q > K means net reverse, which uses NO₂.
Q no longer equals K, so every concentration changes until it does.
Replacing N₂O₄ means making N₂O₄, which uses NO₂.

why.correct: Q<sub>c</sub> = [NO₂]² / [N₂O₄] = (0.0100)² / 0.0400 = 2.50 × 10⁻³. That is less than K = 4.6 × 10⁻³, so the net reaction goes forward, replacing some of the removed NO₂.
For a temperature change, K itself changes. Endothermic: K rises on heating, so Q (unchanged) is now below K, and the net reaction goes forward.
options: Right: here K changes, not Q. With the old concentrations, Q is now less than the new, larger K.
Heating a sealed flask does not change the concentrations at once, so Q does not change. K does.
A temperature change does change K. A justification must say so.
For an endothermic reaction, heat is like a reactant, not a product.

why.correct: A full-credit justification compares Q with K: here Q = 1.6 < K = 4.0, so the net reaction goes forward.
options: Right: claim (direction), evidence (the value of Q from the counts) and reasoning (comparison with the unchanged K).
K does not change with concentration. This answer would lose the point.
Systems do not "want" anything; a justification needs Q compared with K.
This is rate language alone. On the exam, a shift is justified with Q vs K.

why.correct: Q < K, so the net reaction goes forward: Y₂ falls, XY rises, and X₂ falls from 5 but stays above the original 2, because the shift only partly counteracts the change.
options: Right: the shift uses part of the added X₂ (so X₂ ends above 2), uses some Y₂ (below 2) and makes XY (above 4).
The added X atoms cannot vanish; the new equilibrium has a different composition with the same K.
This describes a reverse shift, but Q < K after adding X₂.
With Q < K there must be a net forward reaction, which changes Y₂ and XY as well.

why.correct: The rate picture and the Q picture agree: Q < K is the same situation as forward rate > reverse rate.
options: Right: more X₂ means more X₂-Y₂ collisions each second. This matches Q < K.
The reverse reaction uses XY, which is unchanged at that instant.
Only the forward reaction uses X₂.
The forward rate depends on [X₂], which has risen.

why.correct: Here Q = P<sub>CO₂</sub>. Pumping out CO₂ makes Q < K, so the net forward reaction makes CO₂ until P<sub>CO₂</sub> = K<sub>p</sub> again, the same pressure as before.
options: Right: with Q = P<sub>CO₂</sub>, removing gas makes Q < K and the net reaction goes forward.
Removing a gas changes Q, not K.
The solids are not in Q, but CO₂ is, and it changed.
Lowering P<sub>CO₂</sub> lowers Q.

why.correct: Each concentration doubles. Q<sub>new</sub> = (2[NH₃])² / ((2[N₂])(2[H₂])³) = 4/16 × Q<sub>old</sub> = 0.25 Q<sub>old</sub>. Q < K, so the net reaction goes forward, toward fewer gas moles.
Temperature changes K. For an exothermic forward reaction, K is larger at lower temperature, so Q (unchanged) < K and the net reaction goes forward.
options: Right: cooling favors the exothermic direction, which shows up as a larger K.
For an exothermic reaction, cooling increases K.
Cooling changes K, not Q (the concentrations do not change at that instant).
K depends on temperature, so it changes.

why.correct: A justification names what changed (Q, or K for a temperature change) and compares Q with K to give the direction.
options: Right: names the change in Q and compares it with K.
Right: identifies that K changes with temperature and uses the comparison.
K does not change with concentration.
This restates Le Châtelier without evidence or reasoning; readers do not award it.

why.correct: Calculate the new Q rather than guessing. The factors of 4 on top and bottom cancel, so Q still equals K and there is no shift.
options: Product was added in the same proportion; Q is unchanged.
Reactant was added in the same proportion; Q is unchanged.
K does not change with concentration.

why.correct: Claim, evidence and reasoning: what changed, the comparison, the direction, and when it stops.
AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻; [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = s. K<sub>sp</sub> = s² = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, so s = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.3 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M.
Ag₂CrO₄(s) ⇌ 2 Ag⁺ + CrO₄²⁻; [Ag⁺] = 2s, [CrO₄²⁻] = s. K<sub>sp</sub> = (2s)²(s) = 4s³ = 1.1 × 10⁻¹², so s³ = 2.75 × 10⁻¹³ and s = 6.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M.
Ranking by K<sub>sp</sub> works only for salts with the same ion ratio. Otherwise, calculate the molar solubility of each.
options: Right: 6.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M versus 1.3 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M. With different ion ratios, the K<sub>sp</sub> expressions have different forms, so K<sub>sp</sub> alone cannot be compared.
AgCl has the larger K<sub>sp</sub>, but the expressions differ (s² vs 4s³). Calculate s for each.
Sharing a cation does not make solubilities equal.

why.correct: When two salts produce the same number and ratio of ions, their K<sub>sp</sub> expressions have the same form, so K<sub>sp</sub> ranks solubility directly.
options: Right: both are 1 : 1, so K<sub>sp</sub> = s² for each and a larger K<sub>sp</sub> means a larger s.
These have different ion ratios (1 : 1 and 2 : 1), so their expressions differ.
Different ion ratios: s² versus 4s³.
Different ion ratios: 4s³ versus s².

why.correct: Ions dissolve in the ratio of the formula: 3 M²⁺ to 6 X⁻ is 1 : 2, matching the charges: MX₂.
options: Right: the solution holds twice as many X⁻ as M²⁺, and the charges balance as 2+ and 2(1−).
MX would give equal numbers of each ion and leave a 1+ charge per formula unit.
This would give more cations than anions, the opposite of the diagram.

why.correct: A saturated solution is an equilibrium between solid and ions. Adding solid leaves Q = K<sub>sp</sub>, so the dissolved concentrations stay the same.
options: Right: the solid is left out of Q and K<sub>sp</sub>, so adding it does not change Q; the ion concentrations are already at their equilibrium values.
The dissolving rate and the precipitation rate are already equal. More solid does not change the ion concentrations at equilibrium.
Q still equals K<sub>sp</sub>; there is no net precipitation.
The amount of a pure solid does not enter K<sub>sp</sub>.

why.correct: Like any equilibrium, a saturated solution is dynamic: dissolving and precipitation continue at equal rates.
options: Right: a saturated solution is a dynamic equilibrium between dissolving and precipitation.
Ions keep dissolving; just as many rejoin the solid each second.
Then the concentrations would keep rising and the solid would disappear.
Dissolved ions keep colliding with the solid surface and sticking to it.

why.correct: K<sub>sp</sub> is the product of the ion concentrations, each raised to its coefficient; the solid is left out.
options: Right: the solid is left out, and each ion is raised to its coefficient.
The solid is a pure solid, so it does not appear in K<sub>sp</sub>.
Coefficients are exponents, not multipliers.
Each concentration must be raised to its coefficient.

why.correct: Compare the ion product Q with K<sub>sp</sub>. After mixing, [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M; Q = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ > K<sub>sp</sub>, so solid AgCl forms until Q = K<sub>sp</sub>.
options: Right: mixing equal volumes halves each concentration to 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M, and Q = (1.0 × 10⁻⁴)² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ > 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰.
Compare powers of ten: 10⁻⁸ is larger than 10⁻¹⁰.
The conclusion is right but Q is wrong: mixing equal volumes halves each concentration before you multiply.
Dilution matters only through Q; here Q is still far above K<sub>sp</sub>.

why.correct: Equation, ion concentrations in terms of s, K<sub>sp</sub> expression with exponents, solve.
K<sub>sp</sub> is an equilibrium constant, so it changes with temperature. For endothermic dissolving, heating increases K<sub>sp</sub> and the solubility.
options: Right: for an endothermic dissolving process, K<sub>sp</sub> rises with temperature, so Q < K<sub>sp</sub> and more solid dissolves.
A larger K<sub>sp</sub> means more ions can be in solution, so solid dissolves rather than precipitates.
K<sub>sp</sub> is constant only at a fixed temperature.
Warming does not change the ion concentrations at once, so Q does not change. K<sub>sp</sub> does.

why.correct: Ag₃PO₄(s) ⇌ 3 Ag⁺ + PO₄³⁻. [Ag⁺] = 3s, [PO₄³⁻] = s. K<sub>sp</sub> = (3s)³(s) = 27s⁴ = 27(4.3 × 10⁻⁵)⁴ = 9.2 × 10<sup>−17</sup>.
In a saturated solution the ion concentrations are fixed by K<sub>sp</sub> at a given temperature. More water dissolves more solid in total, but the concentrations come back to the same values.
options: Right: each AgCl that dissolves gives one of each ion.
Right: once saturated again, the concentrations return to the values set by K<sub>sp</sub>.
The solid is not in K<sub>sp</sub>; its amount does not matter.
Dissolving continues, balanced by precipitation at the same rate.

why.correct: This is the common-ion effect: an ion already present (Cl⁻ from NaCl) lowers the solubility of a salt that contains it.
options: Right: the solubility falls from 1.6 × 10<sup>−2</sup> M in water to 2.7 × 10<sup>−4</sup> M in 0.25 M NaCl.
The numbers fall, not rise, as [NaCl] increases.
The solubility changes by a factor of about 60 across the table.
The trend is right, but the cause is wrong: K<sub>sp</sub> is the same in every solution at 25 °C.

why.correct: Reason with Q and K<sub>sp</sub>: Cl⁻ from NaCl raises Q, so the equilibrium sits further toward the solid and less PbCl₂ dissolves.
options: Right: with Cl⁻ already present, a smaller [Pb²⁺] is enough to make Q reach K<sub>sp</sub>.
K<sub>sp</sub> depends only on temperature; the common ion changes Q.
Na⁺ is a spectator ion here. The shared ion, Cl⁻, is what matters.
The solutions are dilute; the effect is an equilibrium effect of Cl⁻, not a shortage of water.

why.correct: Always check the approximation. Here 2s would be 0.34 M, far more than 5% of 0.010 M; the exact solution (about 1.3 × 10<sup>−2</sup> M, below the pure-water value) needs the full expression.
options: Right: 2s would be 0.34 M, far more than 0.010 M, so 0.010 + 2s is not ≈ 0.010. A solubility above the pure-water value is a sure sign.
Squaring was done: 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ / (0.010)² = 0.17. The problem is the approximation itself.
The 4 appears only when [Cl⁻] = 2s with no other source of Cl⁻.
A common ion can only lower solubility; 0.17 M is ten times the pure-water value, so something is wrong.

why.correct: A common ion raises Q above K<sub>sp</sub>, so solid forms until Q = K<sub>sp</sub> again; K<sub>sp</sub> itself is unchanged.

variables.name: [Pb<sup>2+</sup>]
variables.why: Added Cl⁻ makes Q > K<sub>sp</sub>, so PbCl₂ precipitates, removing Pb²⁺.

variables.name: [Cl<sup>−</sup>]
variables.why: Some added Cl⁻ precipitates, but most stays: the shift only partly counteracts the change.

variables.name: Mass of solid PbCl<sub>2</sub>
variables.why: Precipitation adds to the solid.

variables.name: K<sub>sp</sub>
variables.why: Same temperature, same K<sub>sp</sub>.

why.correct: Any common ion lowers solubility. Because [Ag⁺] is squared in K<sub>sp</sub>, adding Ag⁺ cuts the solubility more than adding the same concentration of CrO₄²⁻.
options: Right: 6.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M in water, 2.3 × 10<sup>−6</sup> M with chromate, 4.4 × 10<sup>−10</sup> M with silver. Ag⁺ is squared in K<sub>sp</sub>, so the silver common ion lowers solubility far more.
Both common ions lower solubility, but Ag⁺ (squared in K<sub>sp</sub>) has the larger effect, so beaker 2 is lowest.
Common ions lower solubility, so water gives the highest value, not the lowest.
K<sub>sp</sub> is the same in all three, but solubility is not.

why.correct: K<sub>sp</sub> changes only with temperature. In beaker 2, [Ag⁺] is high and [CrO₄²⁻] low, but [Ag⁺]²[CrO₄²⁻] is still 1.1 × 10⁻¹².
options: Right: both are at 25 °C. The common ion changes the solubility, not K<sub>sp</sub>.
Less solid dissolves, but the ion concentrations still multiply to the same K<sub>sp</sub>.
[Ag⁺] is larger and [CrO₄²⁻] is smaller; the product is unchanged.
K<sub>sp</sub> uses the total [Ag⁺], whatever its source.

why.correct: Only an ion that appears in the solubility equilibrium (Ca²⁺ or F⁻) raises Q and lowers the solubility. Of these, only NaF supplies one.
options: Right: it supplies F⁻, a common ion.
Neither Na⁺ nor Cl⁻ is in the CaF₂ equilibrium, so Q is unchanged.
Neither K⁺ nor NO₃⁻ is in the CaF₂ equilibrium.
A nonelectrolyte adds no ions, so it does not change Q.

why.correct: Adding a common ion raises Q above K<sub>sp</sub>; the net reaction is precipitation, which lowers [Ba²⁺] until Q = K<sub>sp</sub>.
options: Right: claim (precipitate forms), evidence (sulfate added), reasoning (Q > K<sub>sp</sub>).
K<sub>sp</sub> does not change with concentration, and adding a common ion lowers solubility.
Na⁺ is a spectator; the solid stays BaSO₄.
Rate language alone does not earn the point; compare Q with K<sub>sp</sub>.

why.correct: The common ion sets one concentration; the small-x approximation from topic 7.7 makes the algebra simple; always check it.

Precipitation happens when dissolved ions meet the solid. A higher concentration of one of the ions speeds precipitation, so the dissolving and precipitation rates become equal with less salt dissolved.
options: Right: the precipitation rate rises with the ion concentration, so less salt needs to dissolve before the rates match.
Dissolved ions do not coat the solid; the effect comes from the equilibrium.
Dilute ions barely change water as a solvent.
The solid is the same compound; only the balance between dissolving and precipitation changes.
